title: Efficient electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol on Cu nanoparticles decorated on N-doped graphene oxide catalysts
abstract: Efficient electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol is a promising approach for obtaining high-density renewable energy storage and relieving environment stress. In this paper, we report the highly efficient electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol by using Cu nanoparticles decorated on pyridoxine modification graphene oxide sheets (GO-VB6-Cu) as robust electrocatalysts. CO2 was efficiently reduced to ethanol in 0.1M KHCO3 solution by using GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst at an overpotential as low as 0.140 V. The maximum Faradaic efficiency for ethanol formation of 56.3% was obtained at the potential of −0.250 V vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode. The resultant nanocomposite presented no degradation after approximately 24 h of continuous operation, demonstrating the pronounced stability of the electrode. The notable reactivity toward CO2 reduction achieved here can be ascribed to large electrochemically active surface area, enhanced CO2 adsorption, and low electron transfer resistance.

A B S T R A C T
Efficient electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol is a promising approach for obtaining high-density renewable energy storage and relieving environment stress. In this paper, we report the highly efficient electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol by using Cu nanoparticles decorated on pyridoxine modification graphene oxide sheets (GO-VB6-Cu) as robust electrocatalysts. CO2 was efficiently reduced to ethanol in 0.1M KHCO3 solution by using GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst at an overpotential as low as 0.140 V. The maximum Faradaic efficiency for ethanol formation of 56.3% was obtained at the potential of −0.250 V vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode. The resultant nanocomposite presented no degradation after approximately 24 h of continuous operation, demonstrating the pronounced stability of the electrode. The notable reactivity toward CO2 reduction achieved here can be ascribed to large electrochemically active surface area, enhanced CO2 adsorption, and low electron transfer resistance.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The accelerated consumption of fossil fuel resources has resulted in the rising level of atmospheric CO2, leading to energy crisis and global warming. Thus, converting CO2 to value-added products has attracted considerable attention. Electrochemical reduction of CO2 into chemical fuels is an attractive option to simultaneously solve the above two problems. [1–4] In addition, the electrochemical conversion system can operate under ambient conditions and utilize electricity supplied by sustainable renewable sources, such as solar and wind [5,6]. However, the electrochemical reduction of CO2 as an “artificial photosynthesis” process is limited by the lack of electrocatalysts that are energetically efficient, low cost, and highly stable. [3,7,8]
Among various CO2 reduction products, ethanol is a promising product owing to its high energy density, safety, and easy storage. [5,9,10] Efficient electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol is an attractive technique for converting CO2 into reusable carbon forms, creating a sustainable carbon recycling system. Various electrocatalysts such as transition metals [11], transition metal oxides [12], metal alloys [13], and heteroatomic carbon nanomaterials [14], have been utilized for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol. Among these materials, Cu-based materials have attracted considerable attention owing to their unique electrocatalytic behavior in enabling adsorbed CO* to further generate reduced organic molecules, such as
ethanol and methanol, but at large overpotentials. [15,16] Cu-based carbon catalysts, such as oxide-derived Cu/carbon [17] and Cu-carbon dots [18], exhibit dramatically improved efficiency for CO2 reduction at low overpotentials and excellent stability relative to metal Cu electrodes.
Relative to metal-based catalysts, carbon-based materials possess exceptional electronic and physical properties, such as high charge mobility, high specific surface area, and good thermal conductivity. [19–21] Graphene-based materials have received much attention in recent years and have been considered as promising candidates for different electrocatalysts in miscellaneous electrochemical applications. Recently, N-doped graphene materials have been extensively investigated because of their high catalytic properties for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. For instance, Ensafi et al. [22] synthesized Pt-modified nitrogen-doped reduced graphene oxide (GO) as the electrode for the reduction of CO2 to methanol with a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 41% at an applied potential of −0.30 V vs. Ag/AgCl. Rondinone et al. [23] reported Cu nanoparticles (NPs) decorated on a highly textured N-doped carbon nanospike film (Cu/CNS) for the direct electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol with a high FE of 63% at −1.2 V vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) (but a relative high overpotential). N-doped graphene materials are excellent alternative electrode materials relative to metal-based materials, which are readily prepared and provide abundant functional groups for further

electrochemical reaction. In general, N atoms are incorporated into the graphene lattice to develop N-doped graphene materials. However, chemical vapor deposition [24,25], thermal annealing of graphene or GO with NH3 [26,27], and arc discharge of graphite with pyridine/NH3 [28] are laborious and time-consuming preparation processes that require special expensive instruments under harsh synthetic conditions. In addition, the materials prepared using these approaches suffer from the drawbacks of various functionalized N formation species (pyridinic N, pyrrolic N, graphitic N, and N-oxide), which can severely affect product selectivity, due to a variety of active centers. Nevertheless, simple and facile synthetic methods are generally used to introduce Ncontaining precursors modified onto the surface of graphene to obtain N-doped graphene materials [29,30]. Such facile and simple preparation processes can facilitate the generation of single N species on the graphene surface for the effective control of product selectivity. Moreover, the nature of N functionalities and the N-doped level are greatly affected by the structure of N-containing precursors, suggesting that the rational selection of a proper N source is an effective way to enhance the catalytic activity of N-doped graphene. Pyridoxine (VB6), as an N-containing precursor, is an important biologically active compound. It could be functionalized on the surface of carbon materials, such as carbon nanotube, graphene, and carbon fiber, forming single N species catalysts. Such a unique structure could provide extraordinary catalytic ability, as confirmed by our previous work. [31] In addition, the applicability of graphene is encumbered by overcoming the high cohesive van der Waals energy (5.9 kJ mol−1 carbon) among the graphene sheets. [32] Therefore, the most conventional synthetic route for N-doped graphene is from GO [33], the oxidative product of graphite, which contains a large number of carboxyl groups at the edges. These groups serve as reaction sites for functional modification, such as N functionalization [34,35].
Along this direction, a series of VB6-functionalized GO (GO-VB6) materials was synthesized in our previous work to catalyze CO2 reduction, showing excellent efficiency (maximum FE of ethanol achieved 36.4%) but slightly high overpotential (maximum FE of ethanol obtained at the overpotential of 0.490 V) [31]. To address this problem, we developed Cu NPs dispersedly loaded on the sheet-like VB6-modified GO (GO-VB6-Cu) materials and successfully controlled the amounts of Cu loaded in the present work. The resultant materials were evaluated as efficient and robust electrocatalysts for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol in 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. GO-VB6-Cu with 10 wt% Cu NPs loading amount showed a high catalytic ability for the conversion of CO2 to ethanol with FE as high as 56.3% at an applied potential of −0.250 V vs. RHE. This applied potential exhibited a lower overpotential of 0.950 V than Cu/CNS material. [22] Compared with the electrochemical characterization of GO-VB6-Cu with that of GOVB6, [31] the presence of Cu NPs in these novel nanostructured catalysts could lower the ethanol formation overpotential and further improve the ethanol formation efficiency. The correlation of Cu metal, VB6 precursor, and GO sheets in the resultant materials with CO2 reduction activity was also explored. Electrochemical kinetic data were employed to analyze the possible mechanism for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol on GO-VB6-Cu.

sections.heading: 2.1. Chemicals
sections.text:
VB6 (purity> 98%) was obtained from Macklin. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), sulfoxide chloride (purity> 99%), N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF, purity> 99.5%), glacial acetic acid (purity> 99.5%), ethyl acetate (purity> 99.5%), hydrazine hydrate (N2H4•H2O (50 wt%)), ethylene glycol (EG, purity> 99.0%), and copper nitrate trihydrate (AR) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co.. The commercial GO was obtained from Beijing HWRK Chem Co., LTD. Nafion® 117 solution (5%) and Nafion 117 membrane were obtained
from Dupont. Carbon paper (CP, HCP010) was purchased from Shanghai Hesen Electrical Co..

sections.heading: 2.2. Materials characterization
sections.text: Crystal-phase X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded using an Ultima IV X-ray powder diffractometer equipped with Cu Kα radiation (k =1.5406 Å). Microstructure and energy dispersive X-ray (EDX, Oxford; UK) mapping were analyzed using Hitachi S-4800 field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) equipped with an EDX fluorescence spectrometer. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) patterns and the average particle sizes were recorded by TECNAI G2F30 transmission electron microscope. The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed on the Thermo Scientific ESCA Lab 250Xi using 200W monochromatic Al Kα radiation. The 500 μmX-ray spot was used. The base pressure in the analysis chamber was about 3× 10−10 mbar. Typically, the hydrocarbon C1s line at 284.8 eV from adventitious carbon was used for energy referencing. All the electrochemical experiments were performed using a CHI 660C electrochemical station (Shanghai Chenhua Instrument Co. Ltd).

sections.heading: 2.3. Material synthesis
sections.text: The GO-VB6 material, as the precursor material, was synthesized in previous report. [32] The GO-VB6-Cu materials employed the following synthetic process. In brief, GO-VB6 (10mg) was dispersed into the EG via sonication for 60min to form the homogeneous turbidity, and then the EG solution of Cu(NO3)2 was added dropwise. Next, N2H4•H2O was added under stirring. The molar ratio of N2H4•H2O to Cu2+ ions was 20:1. Finally, the reaction was conducted at 60 °C for 24 h. The obtained material was recovered by centrifugation, washed with the deionized water, and then dried in an oven at 40 °C. By changing the Cu (NO3)2 concentration, the materials with different intended Cu contents with 5%, 10%, 20% and 40% were obtained, donated as GO-VB6-Cu-1, GO-VB6-Cu-2, GO-VB6-Cu-3 and GO-VB6-Cu-4. In addition, the synthetic process of GO-Cu material with the Cu content of 10 wt% was similar with the above procedure, but using GO instead of GO-VB6.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical experiments
sections.text:
An H-type cell separated by a Nafion 117 ion exchange membrane was used for all electrochemical experiments at ambient temperature. 0.1 M KHCO3 solution served as the electrolyte. A Pt sheet electrode (2 cm×2 cm) was used as the counter electrode in the anode cell, while the various GO-VB6-Cu, GO-VB6, and GO-Cu catalysts loaded on CP (2 cm×2 cm) formed the working electrode, and the saturated calomel electrode (SCE) was used as the reference electrode in the cathode cell. The working electrode was prepared as following: 10mg of catalyst was suspended into 120 μL of the mixture solution (80 μL of the deionized water and 40 μL of the Nafion®117 dispersion (5 wt%)), and sonicated for 30min to form the catalyst suspension. And then the catalyst suspension was uniformly loaded on the CP and dried in air. Before the electrochemical reduction of CO2, the CO2 gas was passed through the electrolyte for at least 30min to ensure saturation. Liquid phase products were analyzed by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra recorded on an Ascend 400 (400MHz, Bruker, Germany) spectrometer. Typically, the catholyte (200 μL) containing the liquid product was mixed with the D2O solution (200 μL) of 1mM DMSO as internal standards. The 1H NMR spectrum was measured with water suppression via a pre-saturation method. The area ratio of the ethanol peak to the DMSO peak was compared to the standard curve to quantify the concentration of ethanol. The standard curve of ethanol was presented in Fig. S1.
To confirm that the evolved products originate from CO2, isotopic labelling experiments were performed by using isotopic 13CO2 (13C 99%, Sigma-Aldrich) instead of 12CO2 as the carbon source. The liquid
products were analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC–MS, Agilent TRACE 6890/5973 N).
Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was carried out in N2- and CO2saturated 0.1M aqueous KHCO3 solution with a conventional threeelectrode cell comprising a Pt mesh counter electrode, an SCE reference electrode, and the various GO-VB6-Cu, GO-VB6, or GO-Cu catalysts modified the glassy carbon electrode (Diameter =2mm) as the working electrode. The working electrode was prepared by the following text: 1 mg of the GO-Cu, GO-VB6, or various GO-VB6-Cu catalysts was suspended in 40 μL of the deionized water and 20 μL of the Nafion®117 dispersion (5 wt%) forming the mixture solution. After sonification for 30min, 2 μL of the catalyst suspension was dropped onto the glassy carbon electrode and dried at room temperature. In addition, LSV was tested in N2- and CO2-saturated 0.1M KCl aqueous solution. The potential, measured against an SCE electrode, was converted to the potential versus RHE according to the equation:
E (RHE) = E (SCE) + 0.059 × pH+0.241 Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted at the
open circuit potential in N2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution with the AC amplitude of 5mV and a frequency range between 100 kHz and 0.1 Hz. In this work, the glassy carbon electrode loaded with the GO-Cu, GO-VB6, and GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalysts, an SCE, and a Pt sheet were used as the working electrode, the reference electrode, and the counter electrode, respectively. With regards to preparing the glassy carbon working electrode, the preparation process was the same as that of LSV.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
The typical synthesis processes for GO-VB6-Cu catalysts are presented in Scheme 1. GO-VB6 catalyst was prepared as described in a previous study [31], where VB6 was successfully grafted onto GO, which was confirmed by XPS, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, XRD, and elemental analysis. Subsequently, Cu NPs covering on the entire GO-VB6 substrates were generated by a simple chemical co-reduction route (N2H4•H2O and EG as the co-reduction agents). XRD characterization was adopted to gain insights about material composition (Fig. 1A). For reference, GO-VB6 was used and showed only the peak of C (denoted by diamond). The XRD pattern of GO-VB6-Cu-1 only showed a weak characteristic peak of Cu at 2θ=43.3°. The other three GO-VB6-Cu materials exhibited the expected peaks for metal Cu at 2θ=43.3°, 50.5°, and 74.1°, which were represented by the dashed lines. A set of Cu peaks emerged remarkably with increasing contents of Cu, which coincided with the data of EDX mappings of Cu element for various GO-VB6-Cu materials (Fig. S2). The additional Cu2O peak (represented by the solids lines) at 2θ=36.7° appeared in the XRD patterns of GO-VB6-Cu (Fig. 1A).
XPS analysis of GO-VB6-Cu materials was employed to explore further the composition and surface state. For simplicity, the GO-VB6Cu-2 material served as the example in the following text. As expected, XPS analysis of GO-VB6-Cu-2 in Fig. 1B showed the signal peaks of C, O,
N, and Cu species, which demonstrated two points. First, VB6 was successfully modified on GO, as evidenced from the pyridinic N peak at ˜399.1 eV in the N1s spectrum (Fig. 1C). Second, Cu species were present in GO-VB6-Cu-2. The high-resolution Cu2p XPS spectrum in Fig. 1D exhibited binding energies at 932.5 and 952.5 eV, which could be assigned to Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2, [36,37] respectively. These energies indicated the presence of Cu metal. The slight binding energy peak at approximately 933.3 eV associated with Cu2O, corresponding well with the XRD results.
Morphologies of GO, GO-VB6 nanosheets, and the deposition of various Cu NPs were characterized by TEM. The TEM images in Figs. 2A and 2B show GO nanosheets with a typical crumpled surface and GOVB6 nanosheets with a transparent paper-like structure, respectively. The TEM images of various GO-VB6-Cu materials in Figs. 2C-F and S3 display Cu particles with nanosize and irregular shape that are uniformly coated on the surface of GO-VB6 nanosheets. Those TEM images also exhibit distinguished differences in individual particle size. The sizes of Cu NPs were distinctly controlled by increasing the weight ratios of Cu during material synthesis. The particle size histograms inserted in Fig. 2 express a detailed information about size distribution. No dramatic differences in Cu particle size distributions (2–12 nm) were found between GO-VB6-Cu-1 and GO-VB6-Cu-2, but the well-dispersed Cu particles of the latter revealed slightly denser evenly packed on the surface of GO-VB6 nanosheets than those of the former, as shown from Figs. 2C, D and S3A, B. However, when the Cu content was increased to 20 wt%, GO-VB6-Cu-3 yielded much more and larger Cu NPs with a size distribution between 5 and 50 nm, accumulating into clusters, as displayed in Figs. 2E and S3C. As expected, the GO-VB6-Cu-4 catalyst presented the largest Cu NPs with the broadest size distributions (25–200 nm) and large amounts of Cu NP agglomeration on the GO-VB6 surface (Figs. 2F and S3D).
Linear sweep voltammograms acquired in N2- and CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution are recorded in Fig. 3, indicating the remarkable differences in electrocatalytic abilities among various GO-VB6-Cu catalysts. Fig. 3 illustrates the monotonous raise in the reductive current densities (J) under N2 atmosphere in the entire potential range for all GO-VB6-Cu catalysts, which could be mainly ascribed to hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) [38]. When the gas supply was changed to CO2, an obvious reduction peak appeared, indicating that CO2 was reduced on GO-VB6-Cu. Intriguingly, more negative potentials for HER were observed in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution than in N2-saturated 0.1M KHCO3 solution among all GO-VB6-Cu catalysts, illustrating that the presence of CO2 inhibited the HER and facilitated CO2 reduction. Notably, the electrocatalytic abilities for CO2 reduction on the GO-VB6-Cu catalysts were closely associated with the amounts of Cu in the GO-VB6-Cu catalysts. Table S1 shows the different peak potentials and corresponding peak J. As displayed in Fig. 3 and Table S1, the GOVB6-Cu-2 catalyst as the working electrode showed significant electrocatalytic activity for CO2 reduction, i.e., the highest peak J was 7.452mA/cm2 at the lowest peak potential of−0.232 V vs. RHE among all GO-VB6-Cu catalysts.
Scheme 1. Schematic illustration of the process for GO-VB6-Cu preparation.
To shed further light into the catalytic activity of the various GOVB6-Cu catalysts, we conducted potentiostatic electrolysis of CO2 tests in 0.1M KHCO3 solution at the potential range from −0.050 V to −0.450 V vs. RHE. The liquid-phase produce, only ethanol, was detected by 1H NMR, as shown in Fig. S4. CO2 reduction efficiencies on
the GO-VB6-Cu catalysts depended on Cu amounts. The efficiencies over the different GO-VB6-Cu catalysts across the potential range from −0.050 V to −0.450 V vs. RHE are shown in Fig. 4. As expected, the GO-VB6-Cu catalysts with different Cu amounts revealed different electrochemical activities for ethanol formation. The FEs of ethanol formation on the various GO-VB6-Cu catalysts, as the potential shifted to negative position, showed volcanic-type trends (Fig. 4). Notably, the highest FE for ethanol (FEethanol = 56.3%) was obtained at −0.250 V vs. RHE on the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst. The significant performance was comparable to and even higher than those of Cu-based and carbonbased catalysts reported recently, such as Cu/CNS [21], Cu nanowire arrays [39], Cu-Au alloy [40], Cu overlayers on tetrahexahedral Pd nanocrystals [41], Cu2O films [9], CuO NPs [12], oxide-derived copper [2], oxide-derived Cu/carbon [17], and N-doped graphene quantum dots [42], which are summarized in Table S2. CO2 reduction, at GOVB6-Cu-2 catalyst, occurred obviously to ethanol in 0.1 M KHCO3 solution at −0.050 V vs. RHE, corresponding to the overpotential of 0.140 V. The low overpotential of ethanol generation possibly resulted from Cu introduction on the GO-VB6 surface [31].
The enhanced activity for GO-VB6-Cu-2 in all GO-VB6-Cu catalysts might be partially caused by the increased electrochemical active surface area (ECSA), which was tested based on the double layer capacitance (Cdl) in N2-saturated 0.5M H2SO4 solution (Fig. S5). The ECSA could be reflected by the Cdl that was calculated on the basis of the capacitive current (IC) against scan rate. As expected, the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst displayed the maximal Cdl (312 μF/cm2) presented in Fig. S6, which was larger than those of the other GO-VB6-Cu catalysts (i.e., 91.4, 156, and 116 μF/cm2 for GO-VB6-Cu-1, GO-VB6-Cu-3, and GOVB6-Cu-4, respectively). This result indicated that sufficient catalytic
sites for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 were obtained with the substantial increase in ECSA.
Analysis of the reaction products was performed using NMR spectroscopy and GC–MS to confirm that the evolved products originated from CO2. Both methods indicated that the ethanol formed through the electrolysis of a CO2-saturated solution. When N2 was supplied to replace CO2, no liquid products were detectable by 1H NMR (Fig. S7). Then, the isotopic 13CO2 was used as the reactant to trace the carbon sources in the electrocatalytic reaction, and the obtained products were identified by GC–MS (Fig. S8B), comparing with the GC–MS for electrolysis of 12CO2 (Fig. S8A). The GC–MS full spectra in Figs. S8A and S8B display the signals of H2O solvent and ethanol. The detected signals of 13CH313CH2OH (m/z=47, 48) when 13CO2 was used as the reactant significantly differed from those of 12CH312CH2OH (m/z=45, 46) when 12CO2 was used. This result confirmed that the produced ethanol indeed originated from CO2.
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 was performed in 0.1 M KHCO3 and 0.1M KCl solution to study the effect of electrolyte anion types on the catalytic ability of the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst. LSV experiments for the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst were also conducted in 0.1 M KCl solution under N2 and CO2 atmospheres, respectively. As shown in Fig. S9, the results of N2 and CO2 atmospheres in 0.1M KCl solution were similar to those in 0.1M KHCO3 solution. Notably, the reduction peak potential in 0.1M KHCO3 solution was dramatically more positive than that in 0.1 M KCl solution, indicating that 0.1M KHCO3 solution, acting as the electrolyte, was more favorable to the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. Obviously enhanced FEs of ethanol in 0.1M KHCO3 solution
could be achieved, as shown in Fig. S10, compared with those in 0.1M KCl solution. In addition, the overpotential for ethanol formation in 0.1 M KHCO3 solution was lower than the one in 0.1M KCl solution. These findings inferred that 0.1M KHCO3 solution was beneficial to CO2 conversion, which is consistent with the above results. Apart from the ability of the designed electrode catalysts and the changed in working potentials, tuning the composition and nature of electrolytes also affects product selectivity and yield rate. [43] K+, as an alkalimetal cation in aqueous solution, reportedly benefits CO2 adsorption and stabilizes the possible intermediates, such as COOH*, which may facilitate the enhancement for CO2 electrocatalytic ability. [44] The pH of the electrolyte, especially the local pH, plays an important role in the activity and selectivity of CO2 electroreduction. Peter [45] reported that CO2 reduction is usually carried out at close to neutral pH. Gupta et al. [46] presented a mathematical study to reveal that the electrolyte buffer capacity could influence the local pH and then exert a dramatic effect on CO2 electroreduction activity. Relative to chloridion, bicarbonate features a buffer capacity to adjust the pH value of the electrolyte. Therefore, the effect of catalytic ability of the same catalyst in different electrolytes may partially be ascribed to a local pH effect.
To explore the stability of the GO-VB6-Cu catalysts, we performed continuous CO2 electrochemical reduction on the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst at the potential of −0.250 V vs. RHE for a long time. A stable J of 4.571mA/cm2 and the constant FEs remained around 55% for ethanol (Fig. S11A, B), indicating that no observable deactivation occurred on the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst throughout the entire process. Furthermore, the XRD pattern of GO-VB6-Cu-2 after reaction in Fig. S12 showed the
same component as that of the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst before electrolysis, also confirming the excellent stability of GO-VB6-Cu-2.
To investigate the correlation between catalytic activities and structural components of the GO-VB6-Cu catalysts, we synthesized GOVB6 with the same pyridinic N content of 2.30% and GO-Cu with the optimal Cu content of 10%. These two materials were characterized by XPS and XRD. XPS analysis of GO-VB6 (Fig. S13A) showed the existence of N and absence of Cu. Conversely, the GO-Cu catalyst possessed Cu element but no N, as shown in Fig. S13B. Evidently, the high resolution of Cu 2p in the GO-Cu catalyst suggested the presence of Cu metal and Cu2O, consistent with that of the GO-VB6-Cu catalyst, as shown in Fig. S13C. In contrast to that of the GO-VB6 catalyst, the XRD pattern of the GO-Cu catalyst in Fig. S13D typically occurred the corresponding Cu peaks at 2θ=43.3°, 50.5°, and 74.1°. Subsequently, the catalytic abilities for CO2 electroreduction on the GO-VB6 (Fig. S14A), GO-Cu (Fig. S14B), and GO-VB6-Cu-2 (Fig. 3B) catalysts were compared (Fig. 5A). As revealed in Fig. 5A, the onset potential for CO2 electrochemical reduction on GO-VB6-Cu-2 displayed a significant positive shift in comparison to that on GO-VB6 and GO-Cu. As expected, the GO-Cu catalyst exhibited the worst performance for CO2 reduction, i.e., the lowest peak J of 1.170mA/cm2 at the most negative peak potential of −0.420 V vs. RHE. Then, compared with GO-Cu, GO-VB6 showed a slightly positive peak potential at −0.390 V vs. RHE with the increased peak J of 2.218mA/cm2. As expected, the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst presented the largest peak J of 7.452mA/cm2 at an extremely positive peak potential of −0.232 V vs. RHE. Furthermore, the catalytic abilities for CO2 reduction to ethanol were tested on the GO-VB6-Cu-2, GO-VB6 and GO-Cu catalysts at the individual peak potentials, which are presented in Fig. 5B. The GO-Cu catalyst could produce ethanol through CO2 reduction, but the lowest FEethanol of 10.3% was achieved at the most negative potential of −0.420 V vs. RHE. In addition, the GO-VB6 catalyst exhibited enhanced electrochemical ability for CO2 reduction to ethanol with an FEethanol of 36.4% and little acetone generation at the potential of −0.400 V vs. RHE, respectively. [31] By comparison, the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst showed superior catalytic ability for ethanol generation (FEethanol = 56.3%) at the overpotential of 0.340 V. Fig. 5C shows the J vs. time curves of representative electrolysis experiments at the GO-VB6-Cu-2, GO-VB6, and GO-Cu catalysts. Moreover, the total J for GO-VB6-Cu-2 (4.571mA/cm2) was higher than that for GO-VB6 (0.840mA/cm2) and GO-Cu (0.433mA/cm2), suggesting the enhanced catalytic activity of GO-VB6-Cu for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Pyridinic N acts as the active site for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 in GO-VB6 and GO-VB6-Cu, which could improve electronic conductivity. [31,47] In general, metallic Cu form could be considered as the actual active species to activate CeC coupling reactions and further initiate the desired multi-carbon alcohol production [48,49]. Therefore, we deduced that the high catalytic ability of GO-VB6-Cu can be attributed to the simultaneous introduction of pyridinic N and Cu metal.
The increase in ECSA might be one of the main contributors to the enhanced catalytic activity of GO-VB6-Cu because larger ECSA could afford more catalytically active sites for CO2 electrochemical reduction. To verify this viewpoint, we performed cyclic voltammetric tests for GO-VB6 and GO-Cu in N2-saturated 0.5 M H2SO4 solution to determine the ECSA (Fig. S15). The ECSAs for GO-VB6 and GO-Cu were determined by Cdl, as shown in Fig. 6A. As expected, GO-VB6-Cu-2 exhibited a higher Cdl than GO-VB6 and GO-Cu, indicating larger ECSA, and its remarkably larger amount of active sites. Another important contributor to the enhanced catalytic ability of CO2 reduction was CO2 adsorption capacity. In general, an increased CO2 adsorption could unceasingly supply raw materials (CO2) for subsequent CO2 reduction. [48] The corresponding measurement experiments were performed (Fig. 6B), and results showed that the amounts of CO2 adsorption capacity for GO-VB6-Cu-2 were roughly 2.76 and 6.54 times higher than those of GO-VB6 and GO-Cu, respectively. The kinetic of charge transfer at the catalysts/electrolyte interface, as a key contributor, was then
evaluated by EIS measurements in a conventional three-electrode system in 0.1M KHCO3 solution at the open circuit potential. As shown in Fig. 6C, the semicircle radius of the GO-VB6-Cu-2 catalyst was smaller than those of GO-VB6 and GO-Cu, indicating that the GO-VB6Cu-2 catalyst could minimize the resistance for electron transfer, which highly contributed to the enhanced electronic transfer during the electroreduction of CO2. This phenomenon result might enhance the efficiency of CO2 electrochemical reduction.
Stable CO2 reduction efficiency on GO-VB6-Cu enabled the collection of electrochemical kinetic data to probe the possible mechanism of CO2 reduction to ethanol. A Tafel plot for CO2 reduction to ethanol on GO-VB6-Cu-2 is shown in Fig. 6D. As for the electroreduction of CO2, the Tafel slope is a highly valuable parameter to investigate the reduction reaction mechanism. The possibilities for the chemical ratedetermining step of CO2 reduction include single-electron transfer to CO2 (Tafel slope about 118mV/dec) and single-electron transfer to CO2 prior to a chemical rate-determining step (Tafel slope about 59mV/ dec). [48,50–53] The plot for GO-VB6-Cu presented a good linearity with a slope of 72mV/dec, which is close to 59mV/dec. This result suggests that single electron transfer to CO2 is not the rate-determining step for CO2 reduction. [51] The highly efficient for ethanol formation indicates that CeC coupling is the rate determining step [51,53,54]. Electrochemical kinetic data for GO-VB6-Cu support a possible mechanism that involves a reversible electron transfer to CO2 to form adsorbed CO2•− followed by a series of proton− electron transfer processes to obtain CO*. Subsequently, CO* is further dimerized to form OC−CO*, which may be the key rate determining step. The obtained OC− CO* is then protonated and further reduced, resulting ethanol production. A possible CO2 reduction mechanism on GO-VB6Cu is illustrated in Fig. 7. Tafel plots for CO2 reduction to ethanol on GO-VB6 (141mV/dec) and GO-Cu (152mV/dec) are shown in Fig. 6D. Both values are close to the 118mV/dec expected for the rate-limiting single-electron transfer at the electrode. On the basis of these data, the exchange current densities (j0) were 2.36×10−4, 1.18×10−4, and 2.44×10−5 mA/cm2 for GO-VB6-Cu, GO-VB6, and GO-Cu, indicating that the kinetics for CO2 reduction is faster on GO-VB6-Cu than on GOVB6 and GO-Cu. This finding illustrates that compared with GO-VB6 and GO-Cu, GO-VB6-Cu-2 exhibits a much faster electron transfer and hence faster reaction kinetics in CO2 reduction. This result agrees with previous reports [55,56]. Moreover, higher Tafel slopes and lower j0 for GO-VB6 and GO-Cu than GO-VB6-Cu imply that higher overpotentials are needed for these electrocatalysts to activate the catalytic reaction, which fairly correlate with the results of LSV and potentiostatic electrolysis. Electrochemical kinetic studies indicate that the improved catalysis is linked to dramatically increased electron transfer on the surfaces of the GO-VB6-Cu electrodes.
As illustrated in the previous report about GO-VB6 catalysts on CO2 electrochemical reduction, the pyridinic N species are the active sites, and the pyridinic N content is closely associated with the catalytic ability for CO2 reduction. [31] In general, pyridinic N, located at the edge sites or on the carbon-based surface, might adsorb the reaction intermediates (COOH* or CO*) [57]. Moreover, pyridinic N functionalized on GO-VB6 could be assigned to sp2 hybridization, which could enhance electronic conductivity. [47] Fundamental studies demonstrated that stabilizing chemisorbed CO* on the Cu metal is beneficial to increase the CO* surface concentration, thereby promoting those electrochemical reduction of CO2 pathways involving C− C coupling reactions, and simultaneously blocks reaction sites for HER. [44,58] The above results indicate that GO-VB6-Cu provides high conductivity and more active sites for CO2 electroreduction due to the introduction of pyridinic N and Cu metal. Recent studies for related carbon materials, especially N-doped graphene materials, have shown that the pyridinic N active sites could polarize the adjacent carbon atoms. [59,60] The resulting negatively charged N atoms might promote CO2 adsorption on the catalytic surfaces, stabilize the produced CO2%− intermediates, and facilitate CO2 reduction. [59,60] Moreover, the active pyridinic N sites
uniformly distributed on the surface of GO-VB6 sheets could use the reserved lone electron pairs to adsorb the local CO2 and reduce the energy for CO* intermediate formation. [61] The Cu metal and N-doped carbon hybrid structure might also create active sites to the copper for holding strongly CO* to boost CeC coupling to generate alcohol products and inhibit HER [48,49]. In general, the metallic Cu form during this final reductive activation step can be considered as the actual catalyst species promoting CeC coupling or alcohol formation. [48,49]
The formation of CeC bond is the crucial step for CO2 reduction to ethanol, whereas the formation of the adsorbed intermediates CO* by dissociating CO2 for further reaction with available protons is the key initial step for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 [15]. Cu NPs dispersed on the surface of the carbon substrate could create catalytic sites to form CO by dissociating CO2 and then protonate adsorbed CO* to generate ethanol. [17] Moreover, Cu embedding on the graphene surface, due to obvious triple phase boundary, promotes CO2 molecule adsorption on the GO-VB6-Cu surface and CeC bond formation. Additional experimental and theoretical works are needed to illustrate the reaction paths to ethanol formation on GO-VB6-Cu catalysts.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
The sheet-like N-modified graphene oxide by Cu NPs (GO-VB6-Cu) was successfully designed and proposed as an efficient and robust electrocatalyst for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol in aqueous solutions. The targeted catalyst of GO-VB6-Cu-2 exhibited improved catalytic property to catalyze CO2 reduction to ethanol with a low overpotential of 0.140 V and FE of 56.3% at an applied potential of −0.250 V vs. RHE. Furthermore, the prepared catalyst of GO-VB6-Cu-2 displayed superior stability approximately 24 h during CO2 electrochemical reduction. Electrochemical kinetic studies indicated that the improved catalysis was linked to the dramatically increased electron transfer on the surfaces of the GO-VB6-Cu electrodes and revealed that the possible pathway for CO2 reduction on GO-VB6-Cu was CO2 → CO2%− →CO*→(CO)2%→→→CH3CH2OH. The enhanced activity of GOVB6-Cu might be attributed to the large ECSA, enhanced CO2
adsorption, and low electron transfer resistance. This study may open up a new avenue to design Cu modified heteroatomic carbon materials for improving CO2 conversion efficiency.
